intro/hello: Chapter twenty, the last of the course: looking inside language models.
intro/convnets: In C S two thirty one N, we looked inside ConvNets with pictures: filters, saliency maps, images that excite a neuron.
intro/where: Those show where a network looks, not how it computes its answer.
intro/goal: For language models, the goal got harder: read the algorithm out of the weights, like decompiling a program.
intro/name: That is mechanistic interpretability, and in a few years it went from toy models to frontier models.
intro/plan1: We start with the residual stream, and with attention heads split into two circuits.
intro/plan2: Then a real algorithm made of two heads, the induction head, and probes, which test what a model knows.
intro/plan3: Then the obstacle, superposition, and the tool built for it: sparse autoencoders.
stream/recall: Recall the transformer block: attention and an MLP, each adding its output to its input.
stream/flip: In twenty twenty-one, Elhage and colleagues at Anthropic read that the other way round.
stream/stream: Picture one vector per position, running from the bottom of the model to the top: the residual stream.
stream/read: Every layer reads from the stream: a layer norm, then a matrix.
stream/write: And every layer writes to it, by adding. Nothing is overwritten.
stream/sum: So the top of the stream is a sum: the embedding, plus every layer's writes.
stream/out: Multiply it by the unembedding, W U, and you have the logits.
stream/channel: It is a shared channel: one layer can leave a message in a few directions, and a later layer can pick it up.
stream/direct: And since the sum feeds a matrix multiply, each write's direct effect on the output can be read alone.
lens/model: To watch the stream work, we need a model small enough to read completely.
lens/arch: Here is one: two attention layers, one head each, no MLPs, no layer norm, and twenty letters.
lens/data: It was trained on random letters that start repeating, with a period of six to sixteen.
lens/only: Random letters cannot be predicted. The only way to beat a guess is to notice the repeat, and copy.
lens/sum: Its stream is exactly three pieces: the embedding, plus head zero, plus head one.
lens/lens: Now the lo-jit lens: multiply the middle of the stream by W U, and see what the model would say if it stopped there.
lens/input: Feed in twelve random letters, then the same twelve again. Stand on the F in the repeat: next should come P.
lens/x0: After the embedding, P gets about five percent: a blind guess.
lens/x1: After head zero, still five percent. Whatever it wrote was not for the output.
lens/x2: After head one, ninety-seven percent. Head one wrote the answer.
lens/message: So head zero left a message for head one. To read it, look inside the heads.
heads/four: A head has four matrices: query, key, value and output. But they act in pairs.
heads/qk: Queries and keys only meet in one product, W Q K: the Q K circuit. It decides where to look.
heads/ov: Values and output only act together too: W O V, the O V circuit. It decides what to move.
heads/indep: The two are independent: a head could look in the right place and copy the wrong thing.
heads/rank: Both are thirty-two by thirty-two, squeezed through the head's width of sixteen.
heads/read0: Read head zero's Q K circuit on positions alone: every position looks one step back.
heads/stripe: That stripe below the diagonal says it: head zero is a previous-token head.
heads/read1: Now head one's O V circuit, from letters to logits: the embedding, times W O V, times W U.
heads/diag: A bright diagonal: attending to a letter raises that same letter's logit. It copies.
heads/noinput: All of this comes from the weights alone, with no input text.
induction/seen: Put the circuits together, and you get an algorithm.
induction/rule: If you have seen A then B, and now see A again, predict B.
induction/prev: Step one: head zero writes into every position, the letter before me was this.
induction/here: So the earlier P now carries a note: my previous letter was F.
induction/query: Step two: at the current F, head one asks, whose previous letter was F?
induction/key: Its keys read head zero's notes: one head's output is another's input.
induction/found: The earlier P. Head one puts nearly all its attention there,
induction/copy: and its O V circuit copies P into the stream. The prediction: P.
induction/grid: Draw head one's whole attention pattern, and its signature appears: a stripe, one step right of where the repeat began.
induction/name: Elhage and colleagues found this pair in small models trained on real text, and named it the induction head.
induction/score: The induction score measures it: attention on the letter after the earlier copy. Here, zero point eight seven.
phase/watch: How does this circuit appear in training? Watch the loss on the repeat.
phase/plateau: For five hundred steps it creeps down: letters already seen are a little likelier.
phase/cliff: Then, within a few hundred steps, it falls off a cliff, from two point six to below one.
phase/score: In the same window, the induction score jumps from near zero to about zero point seven five.
phase/grids: Before the drop, head one's attention is a blur. After it, a stripe.
phase/why: Why so sudden? Neither head helps alone: one writes notes nobody reads, the other looks for notes nobody wrote.
phase/together: Once both exist a little, the gradient pushes hard on each, and they grow fast, together.
phase/olsson: In twenty twenty-two, Olson and colleagues found this phase change in real models, up to billions of parameters.
phase/icl: In the same window, in-context learning jumped: the models got much better at using earlier context.
phase/evidence: They argued induction heads drive much of it: removing them removed most of it in small models. In large ones, the evidence is correlational.
probes/cheap: Tracing circuits is slow. A cheaper question: is some piece of information in the stream at all?
probes/probe: A probe answers it: freeze the model, and train a small classifier to read a property from its activations.
probes/linear: If a linear one works, the information lies along directions a single matrix could read.
probes/prev: Probe our stream for the previous letter. In x zero, accuracy is near chance.
probes/x1: In x one, after head zero, about eighty-eight percent. Head zero wrote it, as the circuit said.
probes/lrh: Results like this support the linear representation hypothesis: concepts are directions in activation space.
probes/words: Word vectors hinted at it: man to woman points roughly the same way as king to queen.
probes/othello: And a model trained on Othello moves tracked the board linearly, once squares were read as mine and theirs.
probes/caveat: But a probe shows information is there, not that the model uses it.
probes/patch: To test use, intervene: swap in another input's activation, or push along the direction, and watch the output.
superposition/count: If concepts are directions, how many fit in d numbers?
superposition/exact: At exact right angles, only d. A language model surely tracks far more.
superposition/nearly: But in high dimensions, random directions are nearly perpendicular, and their number grows exponentially with d.
superposition/cost: Pack features along them, and you store far more than d. The price: interference, a little of each in the others.
superposition/toy: Toy Models of Superposition, in twenty twenty-two, made it concrete: five features squeeze through two dimensions.
superposition/decode: Compress with W, decode with W transposed, a bias and a ray-loo. Feature one matters most.
superposition/dense: With dense features, the model keeps the two most important, at right angles, and drops the rest.
superposition/sparse: Now make them sparse: each one sits at zero, ninety-five percent of the time.
superposition/pentagon: Train again, and all five come back, as a pentagon, overlapping.
superposition/between: In between, you often get four: two opposite pairs.
superposition/one: Feed in feature one alone. It comes back strong, and its neighbors pick up a small leak.
superposition/relu: A negative bias and the ray-loo cut most of it away.
superposition/rare: Interference hurts when two features are on at once. With sparse features that is rare, so it pays.
polysemantic/neurons: Neurons are special, since the nonlinearity acts on each one alone. The hope: one neuron, one concept.
polysemantic/some: Some neurons are like that. Many are not.
polysemantic/inception: In an image model, Olah and colleagues found a neuron that fires for cat faces, fronts of cars, and cat legs.
polysemantic/poly: Such neurons are polysemantic, and superposition explains them.
polysemantic/setup: Build eight neurons out of sixteen sparse features with known directions.
polysemantic/grid: Every feature pushes every neuron a little, up or down.
polysemantic/one: Take neuron three, and list the inputs where it fires hardest.
polysemantic/mix: Korean, citations, music. No single label fits it.
polysemantic/nothing: Nothing is wrong with it. There are simply more features than neurons.
sae/invert: If activations are sparse sums of feature directions, try running the toy model backwards.
sae/dict: That is dictionary learning: find more directions than dimensions, so each activation uses only a few.
sae/enc: A sparse autoencoder encodes an activation into a much wider vector of features,
sae/dec: then decodes it as a weighted sum of directions, the decoder's columns.
sae/recon: The loss has two parts: the reconstruction error,
sae/l1: and an L one penalty: the sum of the feature activations, times lambda.
sae/push: It charges every unit of activation the same, so small, unhelpful features get pushed to zero.
sae/norm: Decoder columns stay at length one, or the model would cheat by shrinking features and growing directions.
sae/toy: Train one on our eight neurons, and compare its sixteen features with the true ones.
sae/diag: At a good lambda, almost every true feature gets its own. Polysemantic neurons in, monosemantic features out.
sae/tradeoff: Lower lambda: better reconstruction, blurred features. Raise it: clean features, worse reconstruction.
scale/mono: In twenty twenty-three, Towards Monosemanticity trained these on a one-layer transformer.
scale/found: Its features were far easier to name than its neurons: DNA, Arabic script, base sixty-four, Hebrew.
scale/split: As the dictionary grew, features split: one broad feature became several narrow ones.
scale/scale: In twenty twenty-four, it scaled to Claude three Sonnet, with up to about thirty-four million features.
scale/abstract: Many were abstract: one feature fired for a concept in several languages, and in images.
scale/gg: One feature responded to the Golden Gate Bridge.
scale/clamp: Clamp it high, by pushing the stream along its direction, and the model steered every conversation toward the bridge.
scale/ggc: Anthropic offered this Golden Gate Clawed to the public for a day.
scale/handle: Features are not just labels but handles on behavior, and steering is the causal test probes lack.
scale/others: Open A I trained sixteen million features on G P T four, and Google released open ones for Gemma.
limits/micro: Sparse autoencoders are a powerful microscope, with known distortions.
limits/dark: First, dark matter: the reconstruction is never perfect, and what it misses stays unexplained.
limits/splice: Splice the reconstruction into the model, and its loss goes up, sometimes a lot.
limits/rare: The missing part may be rare features, structure that is no sparse sum, or noise. Nobody knows the mix.
limits/basis: Second, features are a choice: dictionary size, penalty, data, even the seed change what you find.
limits/split: Is math one feature, or ten? Both describe the same activations.
limits/labels: Third, a label read off top examples is a hypothesis. It earns trust through interventions.
limits/probes: And for some jobs, like spotting a harmful request, a plain probe trained for it does as well or better.
limits/next: Newer tools trace a computation through features layer by layer, the way we traced the induction circuit.
outro/recap: So, what did we find inside?
outro/stream: The residual stream is a running sum every layer reads and writes; the lo-jit lens reads it early.
outro/heads: Each head is two circuits: Q K, where to look, and O V, what to move.
outro/ind: Two heads make an induction head, which appears suddenly and drives in-context learning.
outro/probe: Probes show what is linearly present. Interventions show what is used.
outro/sup: Models pack more features than dimensions into superposition, so neurons are polysemantic.
outro/sae: Sparse autoencoders pull those features apart, even in frontier models, into handles you can steer.
outro/close: Ten years ago, we asked where a network looks. Now we ask what it computes, and sometimes, we get an answer.
